Trout sweetlips (Plectorhinchus pictus) reaches a maximum recorded fork length of 83 cm [Li = 83 cm], a size that places it among the larger haemulids inhabiting Indo-Pacific coral reefs. This species is characterized by a notably slow life history, with an estimated maximum lifespan of 4,015 days [am = 4,015 days] under stable thermal conditions of 26.3 °C [T = 26.3 °C]. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) was approximately 5.8% [GSI = approximately 5.8%] at a water temperature of 26.3 °C [T = 26.3 °C]. Field observations indicate that females first attain sexual maturity upon reaching a fork length of approximately 40 cm [Lp = approximately 40 cm], a threshold that corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and gamete production. This size-based maturation schedule is typical for reef fishes that experience moderate levels of fishing pressure, as delaying maturity until a larger size allows individuals to accumulate sufficient somatic reserves to support the energetic demands of spawning. The combination of a large ultimate size and a protracted lifespan suggests a bet-hedging strategy, wherein reproductive output is distributed across multiple years to buffer against environmental stochasticity.

Analysis of the length-weight relationship for this species, based on a fitted regression exponent, indicates that the maximum body mass for an individual attaining the ultimate fork length of 83 cm is approximately 7,153 grams [Wwi = approximately 7,153 grams]. In contrast, the mean body mass at the onset of puberty, corresponding to a fork length of 40 cm, is estimated at 855 grams [Wwp = 855 grams], representing roughly twelve percent of the ultimate mass. This substantial difference between mass at puberty and asymptotic mass underscores a prolonged period of somatic growth following the initiation of reproductive activity, a pattern observed in many iteroparous, long-lived teleosts. The wet weight of a newly emerged larva, derived from an estimated egg diameter of 0.85 millimeters, is calculated to be 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], reflecting the modest initial investment per offspring typical of broadcast-spawning marine fishes. The duration of the egg stage, dependent on prevailing temperatures, is approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] when incubated at 26.3 °C [T = 26.3 °C], after which the yolk-sac larva emerges and begins a brief endotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding.

Habitat preferences for P. pictus are closely tied to structurally complex reef environments, where adults are frequently observed sheltering within ledges and crevices during diurnal hours before emerging to forage over sandy flats at dusk. The species exhibits a diet dominated by benthic crustaceans, polychaetes, and small molluscs, which it extracts by rooting through the substrate with its fleshy, protruding lips—a feeding adaptation that gives the species its common name. Juveniles recruit into shallow, turbid inshore habitats, often associating with seagrass beds or marginal rubble zones, where predation risk is lower and prey densities are high. As individuals grow and approach the size of puberty at 40 cm [Lp = 40 cm] fork length, they gradually shift to deeper, more offshore reef structures, a habitat transition that likely reduces intraspecific competition for food and space. This ontogenetic shift is common among haemulids and is thought to be driven by changing metabolic demands and the need to access larger prey items available in the fore-reef environment. The availability of suitable nursery grounds is considered a critical bottleneck for population recruitment.

Reproductive biology in trout sweetlips follows a pattern typical of many tropical serranids and haemulids, with spawning events concentrated during warmer months when water temperatures promote larval survival and growth. Under experimental conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 26.3 °C [T = 26.3 °C], the age at hatching from the fertilized egg has been recorded at approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days], a duration that aligns with the rapid embryonic development observed in other warm-water perciforms. Following the yolk-sac larval stage, the developing fish undergoes a period of rapid growth and morphological transformation, culminating in larval metamorphosis and subsequent recruitment to benthic habitats. The total lifespan, as estimated from otolith microchemistry and field recapture data, reaches 4,015 days [am = 4,015 days] in wild populations, though captive individuals maintained at 26.3 °C have been documented to survive for a similar duration, suggesting that the species' longevity is largely intrinsic and not strongly modulated by environmental stress at a temperature of 26.3 °C [T = 26.3 °C]. The gonadosomatic index was approximately 5.8% [GSI = approximately 5.8%] at a temperature of 26.3 °C [T = 26.3 °C].

Comparative life history analyses reveal that the maximum fork length attained by P. pictus, 83 cm [Li = 83 cm], is near the upper end of the range reported for its genus, with only a few larger-bodied congeners inhabiting deeper continental shelf environments. Such a strategy buffers against the risk of reproductive failure in variable environments, as the loss of any one spawning event does not compromise the entire annual output. The mass at puberty, approximately 855 grams [Wwp = approximately 855 grams], serves as a key demographic parameter for stock assessment models, as it defines the size at which individuals first contribute to the spawning biomass. Protecting individuals until they have reached at least this size is essential for maintaining the reproductive capacity of the population. Ongoing field studies are refining these parameter estimates through direct measurement of gonadal condition across a broader size and age range.
